questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with alcohol-related cirrhosis is admitted with worsening ascites. The family says the client has been sleeping during the day and awake at night. Which finding is an early sign of hepatic encephalopathy?

options.text: A flapping tremor of the hands when the arms are held out
Yellow sclera and skin that have been present for months
A tense, distended abdomen with a fluid wave on percussion
Small red spider-shaped lesions on the chest

rationale.correct: Hepatic encephalopathy: confusion, sleep reversal, asterixis and fetor hepaticus.

perOption.a: Asterixis and subtle confusion or sleep reversal are early signs of rising ammonia.
perOption.c: Ascites reflects portal hypertension and low albumin.
perOption.d: Spider angiomas reflect hormone changes in liver disease.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with hepatic encephalopathy has been receiving lactulose 30 mL four times a day for 2 days. Which finding best shows the medication is working as intended?

options.text: Two or three soft stools a day and clearer thinking
No bowel movement since the drug was started
Ten watery stools a day and new dizziness on standing up
An ammonia level that has risen since admission

rationale.correct: Lactulose is adjusted to 2 to 3 soft stools a day; monitor potassium and hydration.

perOption.a: Lactulose traps ammonia in the bowel and removes it in the stool.
perOption.b: This means it is not working.
perOption.c: Excessive diarrhea causes dehydration and electrolyte loss.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis and tense ascites is starting spironolactone and furosemide. The client asks what to eat at home. Which diet should the nurse expect to teach?

options.text: Sodium limited to about 2 g a day, with adequate protein
A high-sodium diet to replace what the diuretics remove
Unrestricted salt as long as the client takes the diuretics
A protein-free diet to prevent confusion

rationale.correct: Ascites: sodium restriction, diuretics (spironolactone with furosemide) and paracentesis when needed.

perOption.a: Sodium restriction reduces fluid build-up, and enough protein prevents malnutrition.
perOption.d: Severe protein restriction is not recommended; it worsens malnutrition.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis and known esophageal varices suddenly vomits a large amount of bright red blood. The client is pale and drowsy, with a heart rate of 128/min and a blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Protect the airway and prepare for rapid IV access and fluids
Give the scheduled dose of lactulose to prevent confusion
Measure the client's abdominal girth and weight
Teach the client about stopping alcohol to prevent rebleeding

rationale.correct: Variceal bleeding: airway, IV access, blood products, octreotide and urgent endoscopic banding.

perOption.a: Bleeding varices cause aspiration and shock; the airway and circulation come first.
perOption.b: This is not the immediate priority.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with esophageal varices that were banded this week is going home on propranolol. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I won't drink any alcohol from now on."
"I'll take ibuprofen when I get headaches."
"I'll avoid straining when I have a bowel movement."
"This pill lowers the pressure in my varices."

rationale.correct: Variceal bleeding prevention: nonselective beta-blockers, no NSAIDs or alcohol, and avoiding straining.

perOption.a: Alcohol worsens liver disease.
perOption.b: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk; limited acetaminophen may be advised instead.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with cirrhosis and tense ascites is about to have a bedside paracentesis. The client drank a large glass of water an hour ago. What should the nurse ask the client to do just before the procedure?

options.text: Empty the bladder
Drink another glass of water
Lie prone on the bed
Eat a light snack

rationale.correct: Before paracentesis: have the client void, record baseline vitals, weight and girth, and sit the client upright.

perOption.a: An empty bladder reduces the risk of puncturing it.
perOption.c: The client sits upright or in high Fowler's position.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: During a large-volume paracentesis on a client with cirrhosis, 5 L of fluid has been removed. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider right away?

options.text: BP down from 128/78 to 88/50, with a heart rate of 118/min
An abdominal girth that is 14 cm smaller than before the procedure
The client saying that breathing feels much easier now
A small amount of clear fluid leaking at the needle site

rationale.correct: Large-volume paracentesis can cause hypovolemia; albumin is often given.

perOption.a: Removing a large volume can shift fluid out of the vessels and cause hypotension.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with suspected hepatitis has just had a percutaneous liver biopsy. How should the nurse position the client for the next few hours?

options.text: On the right side with a pillow under the rib margin
On the left side with the knees bent toward the chest
Prone, with a pillow under the abdomen and hips
High Fowler's, with the legs raised on pillows

rationale.correct: After a liver biopsy: lie on the right side for a few hours and watch for bleeding.

perOption.a: Lying on the right side presses on the puncture site and reduces bleeding.
perOption.b: This does not compress the site.
perOption.c: This is not the position used.
perOption.d: This does not compress the site.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with chronic hepatitis C is scheduled for a percutaneous liver biopsy tomorrow. The client takes aspirin 81 mg daily and drinks two or three glasses of wine most nights. Which laboratory results are most important for the nurse to review before the procedure?

options.text: PT/INR and platelet count
Serum potassium and sodium
Urinalysis and urine culture
Fasting lipid panel and glucose

rationale.correct: Check coagulation and platelets, and review anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, before a liver biopsy.

perOption.a: The liver is very vascular, and liver disease impairs clotting.
perOption.b: These are less important for bleeding risk.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Review labs before a liver biopsy.

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a 62-year-old client with advanced alcohol-related cirrhosis. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Yellow skin and sclera
A distended abdomen with a fluid wave
Bruising from minor bumps
A high serum albumin level
A low serum ammonia level
Weight loss without any swelling

rationale.correct: Cirrhosis: jaundice, ascites, bruising, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, encephalopathy and varices.

perOption.a: The liver cannot process bilirubin.
perOption.b: Portal hypertension and low albumin cause ascites.
perOption.e: Ammonia rises when the liver cannot clear it.
perOption.f: Fluid retention usually causes swelling and weight gain despite muscle loss.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the morning laboratory results for a 60-year-old client admitted with decompensated cirrhosis. Highlight the abnormal results.

rationale.correct: Liver disease: raised enzymes, bilirubin and ammonia, with a low albumin and a prolonged PT.

perOption.r1: This is elevated, showing liver cell injury.
perOption.r2: This is low (normal about 3.5 to 5.0), showing reduced synthesis.
perOption.r3: This is elevated and causes jaundice.
perOption.r4: This is elevated and linked to encephalopathy.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old client with cirrhosis who was constipated for 4 days and stopped taking lactulose at home is now confused and drowsy, with asterixis and an ammonia level of 120 mcg/dL. Complete the sentence.

content.template: These findings indicate {{b1}}, and the nurse should anticipate a prescription for {{b2}}.

options.text: hepatic encephalopathy
alcohol withdrawal
hypoglycemia
lactulose
a high-sodium diet
a benzodiazepine

rationale.correct: Treat hepatic encephalopathy with lactulose, often with rifaximin, look for triggers such as constipation or bleeding, and avoid sedatives.

perOption.b1:a: A high ammonia with confusion and asterixis indicates hepatic encephalopathy.
perOption.b1:b: Withdrawal causes tremors and agitation, not asterixis with a high ammonia.
perOption.b2:a: Lactulose lowers ammonia, and constipation is a common trigger.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A community health nurse is preparing a teaching session on viral hepatitis for staff and residents of a homeless shelter, where a resident was recently diagnosed with hepatitis. For each type of hepatitis, choose its main route of transmission.

rationale.correct: Hepatitis A and E: fecal-oral. Hepatitis B: blood, sex and birth. Hepatitis C: mainly blood.

perOption.r1:c1: Hepatitis A spreads through contaminated food and water.
perOption.r1:c2: Hepatitis A is not mainly bloodborne.
perOption.r1:c3: Hepatitis A is not mainly bloodborne.
perOption.r2:c2: Hepatitis B spreads through blood, sex and from parent to newborn.
perOption.r2:c3: Blood is one route, but sex and birth are also major routes.
perOption.r3:c2: Sexual and birth transmission occur but are less common.
perOption.r3:c3: Hepatitis C spreads mainly through blood, especially shared needles.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify transmission routes of viral hepatitis.

questions.stem: A new nursing student who has never been vaccinated against hepatitis B asks about the vaccine before starting clinical placements. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "It's a series of doses, and a blood test can confirm immunity."
"One dose before your first placement protects you for life."
"It isn't recommended for students who wear gloves at all times."
"It also protects you against hepatitis C if you are stuck."

rationale.correct: Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for all infants, most adults and all health care workers.

perOption.a: The vaccine is a 2- or 3-dose series, and health care workers often have a titer checked.
perOption.c: It is strongly recommended for health care students and workers.
perOption.d: There is no hepatitis C vaccine.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with acute pancreatitis is restless with severe epigastric pain that goes through to the back. Which position may ease the pain?

options.text: Sitting up and leaning forward
Lying flat on the back
Head lowered below the feet
Lying face down on the bed

rationale.correct: Pancreatitis pain eases with sitting forward or lying curled on the side.

perOption.a: This position reduces stretching of the inflamed pancreas.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Position a client with pancreatitis for comfort.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old client with a history of heavy alcohol use has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea and vomiting. Which laboratory finding best supports a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?

options.text: A serum lipase more than three times normal
A serum amylase that is below the normal range
A blood glucose of 58 mg/dL
A white blood cell count of 3,200/mm3

rationale.correct: Pancreatitis: a raised lipase and amylase, with epigastric pain radiating to the back.

perOption.a: Lipase is the most specific marker of pancreatitis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with severe acute pancreatitis. The heart rate is 124/min, the blood pressure is 92/56, the urine output is 20 mL/hr and pain is 9 out of 10. Which interventions are the priority?

options.text: IV fluid resuscitation and pain control
A low-fat diet started at the next meal
Walking in the hallway every hour
Teaching about alcohol and support groups

rationale.correct: Acute pancreatitis: aggressive fluids, analgesia and bowel rest, then early nutrition when tolerated.

perOption.a: Large fluid shifts can cause hypovolemic shock, and the pain is severe.
perOption.b: Oral intake waits until the client is stable and the pain eases.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On the third day of treatment for severe acute pancreatitis, a client reports tingling around the mouth and in the fingers. The nurse notes muscle twitching and a positive Chvostek sign. The client has been NPO with IV fluids and has a large area of necrosis on the CT scan. Which imbalance does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Hypocalcemia
Hypercalcemia
Hyperkalemia
Hypernatremia

rationale.correct: Pancreatitis can cause hypocalcemia; monitor for tetany and replace calcium as prescribed.

perOption.a: Calcium binds to areas of fat necrosis in pancreatitis, lowering serum calcium.
perOption.c: This does not cause these signs.
perOption.d: This does not cause these signs.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with chronic pancreatitis has pale, greasy, foul-smelling stools and is starting pancrelipase capsules. When should the nurse teach the client to take them?

options.text: With each meal and snack
At bedtime on an empty stomach
Only on days with fatty stools
Once a week on the same day

rationale.correct: Pancreatic enzymes are taken with meals and snacks; the goal is fewer fatty stools and stable weight.

perOption.a: Enzymes must be present with food to digest fats and proteins.
perOption.b: There is no food to digest.
perOption.c: It is taken with every meal.
perOption.d: It is taken with every meal and snack.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A 42-year-old client comes to the emergency department with pain, nausea and a temperature of 38.3 °C (101 °F) that began an hour after a fried-chicken dinner. Which pain pattern is typical of acute cholecystitis?

options.text: Right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder
Left lower quadrant pain with a recent change in bowel habits
Epigastric pain that is relieved by eating food
Pain near the navel that moves to the lower right

rationale.correct: Cholecystitis: right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, a positive Murphy sign, nausea and fever.

perOption.a: Fat makes the gallbladder contract against a blockage, and pain is referred to the shoulder.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On the evening after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a client reports aching pain in the right shoulder. Vital signs are stable, and the abdomen is soft. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Encourage walking; explain the gas from surgery causes it
Notify the surgeon of a likely complication from the surgery
Apply an ice pack to the shoulder for 20 minutes
Keep the client flat in bed until the morning

rationale.correct: Shoulder pain after laparoscopy is common and comes from residual carbon dioxide.

perOption.a: Carbon dioxide irritates the diaphragm and causes referred shoulder pain; walking helps it absorb.
perOption.c: Walking is more helpful for gas pain.
perOption.d: Walking is better than bed rest.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage shoulder pain after laparoscopic surgery.

questions.stem: A client with jaundice from a blocked bile duct is scratching the arms until they bleed. Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care?

options.text: Cool baths with baking soda and keeping the nails short
Hot showers twice a day to soothe the itchy skin on the arms
An alcohol-based lotion applied after bathing
Wool blankets to keep the client warm at night

rationale.correct: Itching from bile salts: a cool environment, soothing baths, short nails and prescribed medications such as cholestyramine.

perOption.a: These reduce itching and skin damage from scratching.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with compensated cirrhosis asks the nurse what to take for occasional headaches. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Use acetaminophen only as directed, at a lower limit, with no alcohol."
"Take as much acetaminophen as you need, since it's gentle."
"Take your acetaminophen with a glass of wine to relax."
"Ibuprofen is a safer choice for people who have liver disease like yours."

rationale.correct: In liver disease, acetaminophen is used cautiously at lower doses, and NSAIDs are generally avoided.

perOption.a: The liver metabolizes acetaminophen, so lower limits (often 2 g a day) reduce hepatotoxicity.
perOption.d: NSAIDs increase bleeding and kidney risk in cirrhosis.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach safe analgesic use in liver disease.

questions.stem: Two toddlers at a child care center have been diagnosed with hepatitis A. Which measure best prevents further spread at the center?

options.text: Handwashing after diaper changes and before food
Having staff wear masks in the classrooms
Screening the staff for bloodborne infections
Avoiding the sharing of needles or razors

rationale.correct: Prevent hepatitis A with hand hygiene, safe food and water, and vaccination.

perOption.a: Hepatitis A spreads by the fecal-oral route.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
